reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .521 and the average exit velocity is 93.1 mph, and those two numbers together make the projection's 45 home runs in 701 plate appearances feel like a reasonable translation rather than optimism. The contact quality is legitimately elite, and a 12.3% walk rate gives him enough OBP cushion that he doesn't need to be perfect in the zone to reach that .364 figure. His chase and whiff rates land right around league average, which means everything here hinges on whether pitchers find a way to exploit him once scouting reports accumulate, because the bat-to-ball profile isn't carrying this — the raw violence is. If the power translates clean, he's a true middle-of-the-order corner bat; if the zone discipline erodes under a full season of targeted attack, the floor is a high-average slugger with a bit fewer walks and fewer home runs, still plenty useful.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-whiff numbers are the one blemish in an otherwise elite Statcast profile, and even they're starting to look like the acceptable cost of doing business. Wood's 20.8% barrel rate and 95.1 mph average exit velocity are both at the very top of the sport, and a 16.8% walk rate pairs with a 21.7% chase rate to show a young hitter who genuinely understands the zone. The 28.6% strikeout rate is the hinge point: if he finds ways to put more balls in play without sacrificing the plate discipline that makes his power translate, the projection's .904 OPS with 40 home runs looks conservative given what the underlying contact quality already says. If the strikeouts don't come down, he's still a middle-of-the-order bat, just a volatile one.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact quality is essentially the same player on both sides of the ball. As a hitter, his .412 xwOBA and 16.5% barrel rate place him among the elite, and a 14.1% walk rate keeps the on-base column honest even when his 30.4% whiff rate costs him. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and 98.1 mph fastball with 2488 rpm of spin describe a genuine ace, and the projection's .288/.394/.547 line across 693 plate appearances is what you get when neither side of his profile is propped up by luck. The one thread to watch is workload management as a 32-year-old returning from Tommy John, because if the Dodgers limit his pitching role, the offensive value is still elite but the full two-way argument gets smaller.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: A 94.3 mph average exit velocity ranks in the 99th percentile, and when you pair that with a 14.8% barrel rate and 53.1% hard-hit rate, the .370 xwOBA stops looking like noise and starts looking like a floor. The whole profile is a blunt instrument built around elite contact quality, and the projection's .271/.350/.489 line across 633 PA reflects that the bat plays even before you add 32 projected stolen bases. The catch is the 27.1% strikeout rate, which keeps that xBA of .277 from fully translating to the surface — if he can't get that whiff rate below its current 28.3%, some of that raw power will keep evaporating against quality spin. But at 24, with this kind of athleticism and a 10.6% walk rate already suggesting he's not completely lost at the plate, you're looking at a legitimate middle-of-the-order shortstop who steals bases on top.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the swing-and-miss is the number that keeps this profile from being a simple story. Walker's 93.1 mph average exit velocity sits in the 96th percentile, and his .355 xwOBA with a .482 xSLG say the damage he does when he connects is backed by both contact quality and barrel rate, not circumstance. The problem is a 35.3% chase rate and 31.2% whiff rate that both sit near the bottom fifth of the league, which is the only thing standing between him and a cleaner, higher-ceiling outcome. If the plate discipline firms up even modestly, the projection of .276/.336/.474 with 30 home runs and 19 steals across 679 PA undersells him; if it doesn't, he's an exciting but volatile second-division regular whose counting stats lean on volume and a speed game that, at 29.2 ft/s, is legitimately among the fastest in the sport.

reports.name: Kade Anderson

Anderson's 12 walks against 119 strikeouts produce a K-BB% that translates to 21.4% in a league where the average starter sits at 13.5%, and his translated walk rate of 2.1 per nine lands more than a full walk below the MLB mean. reports.name: Eli Willits

The .411 OBP and 18% walk rate translate to a 12.7% BB% in MLB-equivalent terms, well clear of the league mean, and the 43 stolen bases tell you the OBP is a weapon he can actually weaponize. The ISO (.201 across A+ & A) softens to .135 in translation, below average, so the question isn't whether the hit tool and plate discipline hold up over 401 PAs with that K-BB% spread. The question is whether the power grows into something that keeps the defense honest as he climbs: if it does, Willits is an everyday shortstop; if it stalls, he's a high-OBP table-setter who needs the speed to stay legitimate, which at this age and this level is still a very workable floor.

What he isn't is a power threat — 86.9 mph average exit velocity and a 3.9% barrel rate are bottom-of-the-league territory, and the .389 projected SLG reflects that honestly. The whole profile hinges on whether that elite plate discipline (a 16.5% whiff rate, a 24.3% chase rate) keeps translating into enough on-base value to offset eight home runs in a full season. If it does, he's a .360-plus OBP middle infielder who runs for 26 bases and makes pitchers work; if the batted-ball ceiling never rises, he's a very good bench piece wearing an everyday jersey.

reports.name: Joe Ryan
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine. At 5.0%, Ryan sits in the 95th percentile, and that one number explains most of what makes a mid-rotation starter functional without elite stuff: he simply doesn't beat himself. The Statcast contact profile is genuinely uncomfortable, with an 11.1% barrel rate and 42.6% hard-hit rate both well below average, and his 93.5 mph fastball isn't missing bats on its own at a 25.9% whiff rate. What he's built is a profile where command suppresses damage even when contact occurs, and the 27.1% strikeout rate is good enough to keep hitters from waiting him out. The whole thing hinges on that command holding: if the walk rate creeps toward league average, the below-average stuff becomes a real problem rather than a managed one.

reports.name: Seth Hernandez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing on the page, and the walk rate is the thing you have to watch. Across A+ & A in 2026, Seth Hernandez has struck out 118 batters in 74 innings, 14.3 per nine, with a K-BB% of 30 that sits in the 99th percentile of his pool, and a 2.4 ERA with a 1.1 WHIP. Translated to a major-league context, that strikeout rate softens to something around league average, and the walk rate, 3.8 per nine in the minors translating to 4.0, is the honest ceiling tax: if the command doesn't sharpen, the swing-and-miss isn't enough to carry a rotation spot. Back-end starter if it comes together; depth arm if it doesn't.

reports.published_report: The contact profile is where Messick earns his keep: a 4.9% barrel rate and 32.6% hard-hit rate that together explain how a 94.1 mph fastball with 2161 rpm spin becomes a 3.09 xERA. reports.name: Wyatt Langford
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a puzzle without a clean answer. Langford's xwOBA sits at .304, well below the production level his projection asks for, and his 6.1% walk rate is the quieter concern, sitting near the bottom of qualified hitters and capping the ceiling on an OBP that already reads as optimistic at .324. The contact-quality numbers are middling across the board: 38.6% hard-hit rate, an xSLG of .412 against a projected .475, nothing that explains 21 projected home runs without some good fortune on batted-ball outcomes. What saves the profile is the 27.7% chase rate, real discipline in the zone, and 28.4 ft/s sprint speed that makes the 14 stolen bases the most believable line on the card. If the gap between xSLG and projected SLG closes toward the Statcast side, you're looking at a second-division regular who earns his spot with his legs and his glove, not his bat.

reports.name: Gabriel Moreno
reports.published_report: The .372 xwOBA tells you something is working, and the whiff rate of 15.9% explains most of it. Moreno makes contact at a rate that puts him in rare company at any position, let alone behind the plate, and his 11.4% walk rate means pitchers don't get an easy out by pitching around him either. The exit velocity at 89.2 mph is ordinary, so the profile isn't built on raw thump — it's built on a catcher who almost never misses, draws walks, and doesn't need to punish the ball to post a .293 xBA. If the contact quality stays where it is, the projection's .807 OPS at 505 plate appearances looks conservative for the position; if pitchers eventually find a way to exploit the lack of over-the-fence thunder, what's left is still a catcher who gets on base.

reports.name: Logan Webb
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries the argument. The catch is that the strikeout side is genuinely thin: a 19.8% K% in the 27th percentile means he's manufacturing outs through contact management, and if his defense or ground-ball shape turns on him in any given stretch, there's no swing-and-miss floor to fall back on. Project him as a durable mid-rotation piece who posts a 3.65 ERA across a full 186.6 innings by being exactly what he is: someone who doesn't walk people, doesn't give up barrels, and lets contact play against him rather than through him.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report:
The walk rate is the whole profile in one number: 13.5% BB%, at the 6th percentile, is genuinely bad, and it's sitting next to a 27.7% Whiff% that says the stuff is real enough to miss bats.

Brown generates whiffs at a rate that most pitchers would be happy with, and his 86.8 mph average exit velocity suggests he limits hard contact when he does get swings, but none of that matters in a start where he issues four free passes before the fifth inning. The projection slots him at a 3.55 ERA over 107.2 IP, which feels optimistic if the command stays this broken, and the xERA of 3.71 with a 13.5% walk rate is a tension that resolves badly the moment hitters stop chasing — his 26.8% Chase% is already near the bottom of the league, meaning he's getting those whiffs in the zone rather than off the plate. What he is if the walks come down even modestly is a genuine mid-rotation piece; what he is if they don't is a high-leverage strikeout arm squeezed into a starting role.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The .529 projected SLG with a .311 OBP tells you everything about the tension here: real pop, genuinely thin plate discipline. His 11.3% barrel rate is legitimate contact quality, but a 41.7% chase rate sitting at the 4th percentile explains why the xBA lands at .228 while the xSLG reaches .437, a gap that wide meaning he does his damage in a narrow band of the zone. Coors Field paper-coats a .269 AVG projection onto contact skills that look a lot worse away from altitude. The profile works if he keeps barreling enough to outrun the chasing; if pitchers learn to live outside the zone against him, there's not enough walk rate, 5.3%, to keep him from becoming a low-end regular who looks like a lot more at home than he is.

reports.published_report: The .409 OBP at AAA is the number that matters, and it's built on a 16% walk rate that translates to 13.1% at the MLB level. reports.name: Chandler Simpson
reports.published_report: Forty stolen bases on a .356 slugging percentage tells you everything about what kind of player this is. The Statcast profile is almost comically lopsided: a 10.7% whiff rate that grades at the 99th percentile, but an 83.9 mph average exit velocity and a 0.0% barrel rate that both sit at the 1st. He makes contact, relentlessly, and does essentially nothing with it when he does. The projection's .294 AVG is believable given the 63rd-percentile xBA, but the .264 xwOBA tells you the contact quality can't sustain the batting average long-term, and a 4.8% walk rate means there's no secondary path to on-base value if the hits dry up. What's left if the speed cools even slightly is a profile with a near-zero power ceiling and no walks to fall back on, which is a bench outfielder at best, a roster problem at worst.

reports.name: Dylan Cease
reports.published_report: A 36.2% strikeout rate at the 99th percentile while running a 10.6% walk rate at the 23rd — that's the whole tension in Dylan Cease's profile, and it's been there for years. The swing-and-miss is genuine: a 35.4% whiff rate pairs with an average exit velocity of 86.1 mph, and hitters are squaring him up at a 4.8% barrel rate, all of which lands in a 2.78 xERA. The walks are the load-bearing flaw; if he can nudge the command closer to league average, he's a legitimate Cy Young conversation starter, and if he can't, he's still a high-strikeout, slightly volatile ace who will post an ERA in the low threes because the contact quality against him is so suppressed. ValuCast's projection of a 2.70 ERA over 176.9 innings leans toward the optimistic scenario holding.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact profile here is genuinely unusual: a 14.9% whiff rate and a 22.4% chase rate, both elite, attached to an average exit velocity of 87.8 mph that sits near the bottom of the league. He makes consistent contact and almost never offers at bad pitches, yet he rarely damages the ball when he finds it. The .283 xBA reflects what that discipline earns him, because pitchers have to throw strikes and he hits those strikes, but the .418 xSLG tells you what happens when a hitter makes great decisions without much thunder behind them. If the speed (21 projected steals) plays in center and the on-base skills hold, he's a useful everyday piece in a rebuilt White Sox lineup; if pitchers start exploiting the soft contact with a steady diet of heaters middle-in, the 7.1% walk rate probably won't carry him.

reports.name: Taj Bradley

Montero doesn't beat hitters, he doesn't walk them. That's a sustainable shape if contact management holds, but a 17.4% strikeout rate gives hitters a long runway to find him once sequencing breaks down or a lineup sees him a third time through. If the contact luck drifts even slightly and the strikeouts don't respond, the ERA climbs faster than the profile suggests because there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him.

reports.name: Didier Fuentes
reports.published_report: A 30.4% strikeout rate with a 3.04 xERA is the profile of a reliever who genuinely misses bats, and Fuentes is doing it at 21 in a competitive Atlanta bullpen. The fastball sits 97.1 mph, and the 28.7% whiff rate holds up even without elite spin, which means the bat-missing isn't just heater velocity doing the work. The walk rate at 7.7% is the one tension in the card — the chase rate is ordinary, so the strikeouts lean on contact-avoidance and swing-and-miss, and if hitters start laying off, the margin between a 3.04 xERA and something uglier shrinks fast. If the command tightens, he's a high-leverage piece; if it stays loose, the projection's 65.5 innings and 2.8 ERA is still a useful middle reliever, just not one you build around.

reports.name: Quinn Mathews
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Mathews is putting up a 3.1 ERA across 92 innings at AAA with 111 strikeouts, but the 5.1 BB/9 translates to 4.6 against MLB hitters in a league where 3.2 is average, and that gap is the ceiling check on everything else. The strikeout stuff holds up on translation too, 10.9 K/9 at AAA becomes 9.2 at the MLB level, a tick above average, and the 1.1 WHIP shows he's limiting damage despite the walks. But a K-BB% that lands right at the MLB mean when you account for the level jump means the margin for error is thin, and if the command doesn't sharpen, the floor is depth, which is where left-handed relievers with persistent control issues tend to settle.

reports.name: Yandy Díaz
reports.published_report: A 14.2% whiff rate at the 94th percentile tells you exactly what Yandy Díaz is: a contact-first first baseman who makes the barrel question irrelevant by almost never missing. His .283 xBA sits at the 90th percentile, and a 47.3% hard-hit rate means the contact lands with enough force to push a projected .824 OPS at 695 plate appearances. The catch is that a 6.8% barrel rate sitting at just the 37th percentile keeps the ceiling capped — he hits the ball hard and often, just not quite often enough in the sweetest spot to be a true middle-of-the-order force. At 34, this profile holds as long as the bat-to-ball skill doesn't erode, and there's nothing in the Statcast card suggesting it's close to eroding yet.

reports.name: LuJames Groover
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP at AAA is the headline, and it's built on real plate discipline, not a BABIP mirage — well, mostly. Groover has drawn 45 walks against 60 strikeouts across 348 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and the translated walk rate of 10.6% clears what a typical MLB hitter produces while the strikeout rate translates to 19.8%, comfortably below the 22.0% MLB mark. The BABIP of .368 is the honest red flag: if that regresses to earth, the .314 average comes with it, and what's left is a decent OBP, a below-average translated ISO of .133, and a profile that fits the bench side of the bench-or-platoon ceiling his numbers already point toward. The discipline is real enough to survive some contact regression, but he needs the hit tool to play above average in the majors for this to be anything more than a useful reserve piece.

reports.name: Aiva Arquette
reports.published_report: The raw power is the only reason to pay attention here. A .223 ISO across AA & A+ in 185 plate appearances translates to a .156 MLB-equivalent, and the MLB walk rate sits at 8.5% while his equivalent comes in at 7.1%, which tells you the discipline isn't going to carry him when the contact thins. The .297 OBP built on a 6% walk rate and a .263 BABIP leaves almost no margin, and twelve stolen bases across AA & A+ add a wrinkle without solving anything structural. The profile hinges entirely on whether the power stays loud enough at higher levels to compensate for an on-base game that currently doesn't exist, and if it doesn't, you're looking at a bench bat whose best asset is one tool that minor-league translations tend to compress.

At 20 years old with 255 plate appearances spread across three levels, Arjun Nimmala is hitting with real authority in the minors, yet that raw power translates to a .144 MLB-equivalent ISO, nearly identical to the .150 MLB average. The walk rate is the quieter virtue: 32 walks in those 255 plate appearances across AA & A+ & A translates to 9.6% at the MLB level, a hair above average, which keeps the OBP floor from collapsing even if the strikeout rate does not improve. Everything here hinges on whether the contact quality holds as pitchers at full AA expose him consistently; if it does, there's a second-division regular hiding in this profile, and if it doesn't, the floor is a bench piece.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA tell the same story: a 3.31 and .283 both sitting at the 79th percentile, a profile that earns its ERA rather than riding strand rate or sequencing luck. What makes it work is control, a 6.6% walk rate that also grades 79th, paired with a 33.4% chase rate that explains why he doesn't need swing-and-miss volume to manufacture weak contact. The 27.9% whiff rate is functional, not dominant, and the 8.1% barrel rate is the one soft spot, a tick below average that keeps the contact quality profile from being as clean as the peripherals suggest. If the chase rate slides, the strikeout rate won't cover for it, and a 3.68 ERA in 134.5 projected innings turns into something more pedestrian than mid-rotation worthy.

reports.name: Owen Caissie
reports.published_report: A 16.0% barrel rate with a 39.0% strikeout rate is the whole tension in one line. The contact is genuinely elite when it connects, 91.8 mph average exit velocity and a 47.3% hard-hit rate, but a whiff rate at the 2nd percentile means he's making contact so rarely that the raw power barely gets to express itself, which is why the xBA sits at .213 despite the xSLG of .424. The projection's .234/.297/.438 line over 377 PA reflects exactly that: a guy who can barrel the ball as well as almost anyone on the roster but gets eaten alive by swing-and-miss. If the strikeout rate doesn't come down, what's left is a platoon corner bat who goes deep occasionally and not much else.

reports.name: Brock Wilken
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, and the batting average is threatening to collapse the whole structure. Wilken has drawn 63 walks in 380 AAA plate appearances in 2026, a 17% clip that translates to 12.9% at the MLB level, well above where most big-league hitters land, but he's hitting .179 with a .230 BABIP and 111 strikeouts, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .147 sits right at the MLB average rather than above it. That's a profile where the discipline is genuine but the bat-to-ball problem swamps it: a 28.2% translated strikeout rate against a 22.0% MLB norm means the walks buy back roughly what the strikeouts spend, and the .321 OBP at AAA already reflects that uneasy arithmetic. If the contact rate doesn't improve, what's left is a bench-depth first baseman whose plate approach is his only carrying tool.

reports.name: Trent Grisham
reports.published_report: The contact profile is a puzzle: an .247 xBA that barely clears league average sitting underneath a .341 xwOBA and 90.9 mph average exit velocity. Grisham puts the ball hard in the air often enough to push expected slugging to .432, but he hits enough weak grounders that the batting average never follows, which is exactly how you get a .217 projection alongside 20 projected home runs. The one number that genuinely stands out is an 18.0% chase rate, a discipline mark that almost nobody matches, and it fuels a 13.0% walk rate that keeps the .320 OBP afloat even when the hits dry up. The whole profile lives or dies on whether he can lift the ball consistently enough to let that exit velocity play — if launch angle regresses, you lose the power without gaining the average, and what's left is a patient, slow corner outfielder hitting .217.

The contact-first shortstop profile is the whole argument here, and the power is what keeps the ceiling in check. Jim Jarvis is hitting .313 at AAA with 46 walks against 55 strikeouts in 348 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 18.9% in a league that runs 22.0%, his walk rate at 10.8% where the field sits at 8.5%. The 32 stolen bases are loud. But six home runs and a .148 ISO at AAA translate to .13 against MLB pitching, and nothing in the shape of this profile suggests that gap narrows.

If the bat-to-ball and speed carry over, he's a low-end everyday shortstop; if a big league defense solves him, he's a reserve.

reports.name: Ryan Jeffers
reports.published_report: A .857 OPS from a catcher playing 361 projected plate appearances is genuinely valuable, and the .371 OBP is what makes it work — he gets on base at a rate that most catchers his age would trade for without hesitation. The 26.3 ft/s sprint speed sits at the 25th percentile, so he's not running anything, but that's not the profile anyway; his job is to get into the box, take his walks, and hit the ball over the fence 16 times. The whole thing hinges on playing time: 361 PA is already a part-timer's share, and any slippage there turns a genuinely useful offensive catcher into a narrower commodity. If he stays healthy and Minnesota keeps running him out there, he profiles as a legitimate second-division regular at the most undersupplied offensive position in the sport.

reports.name: Reinold Navarro
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is electric and the ERA is a mirage. Navarro is punching out batters at 15.5 per nine at A, which translates to 9.5 K/9 in MLB context, but he's walked 56 in 61.7 innings, and that 8.2 BB/9 translates to 7.3 at the big-league level. The K-BB% translation lands at 11.4%, a tick below the MLB mean of 13.5%, which is the real story: all that swing-and-miss is being swallowed by an inability to throw strikes. Everything hinges on command development, and if it doesn't come, what's left is a depth arm, which is precisely where the ceiling already sits.

reports.name: Yolfran Castillo
reports.published_report: Forty-four stolen bases at 19 years old, across A+ & A, is the loud number — and the plate discipline backing it up is what makes it mean something. Across 442 PA, he's walking at 14% and striking out at just 15%, which translates to a contact-and-zone profile that sits below league-average strikeout rate at the MLB equivalent level while his walk rate clears the MLB average. The problem is the bat doesn't carry power: a .117 ISO across A+ & A translates to roughly .095 at the MLB level, well short of average, and if the speed doesn't stick or the arm-at-shortstop question answers itself poorly, there's not enough thump to carry a corner. Either a high-contact, low-power table-setter who profiles at the bottom of a lineup as a fringe regular, or a bench piece whose speed ages out before the bat develops.

reports.name: Noah Cameron
reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA both sitting at the 28th percentile tell you where the actual skill is, and the projection's 4.52 ERA is essentially agreeing with that read. Cameron gets whiffs at a league-average clip, 25.5%, but the 28.4% chase rate is what undercuts it: hitters aren't expanding, so the strikeout rate, 21.4%, never becomes a weapon. The fastball at 92.5 mph grades in the bottom fifth of the league, which means the spin at 2324 rpm has to do the heavy lifting, and right now it isn't lifting enough. He's a back-end starter who eats 165.8 innings and gives you 10 quality starts if the command holds, and a mid-rotation slot in Triple-A terms if it slips.

reports.name: Kevin Kelly
reports.published_report: The 4.2% walk rate is the whole profile in a single number. Kelly lives at the bottom of the velocity and spin charts, with a 93.1 mph fastball, 2121 rpm, and a 19.4% whiff rate that ranks near the floor of the league, but he almost never gives anything away for free, and that control keeps his xERA at 3.69 and his xwOBA at .298, both comfortably above average. If it works, he finishes with a 2.56 ERA and 0.94 WHIP across 70.5 innings, which is what a soft-stuff reliever looks like when he can strand his own mistakes. If contact quality climbs, the 44.9% hard-hit rate is already knocking at the door, and the strikeouts aren't there to bail him out.

The ceiling here is organizational depth, and so is the floor.

reports.name: Daulton Varsho
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .291 and the average exit velocity sits at 86.2 mph, and those two numbers tell you almost everything: he makes decent contact decisions but doesn't hit the ball hard enough to punish pitchers when he does. The 36.4% chase rate compounds it, because a hitter with soft contact can survive a loose zone if he gets to enough counts, and Varsho mostly doesn't. What saves the profile from being purely grim is a 20.1% whiff rate and genuine outfield defense, and the projection's .388 slugging still implies enough pop to keep pitchers honest across 550 PA. If the chase rate comes down and he catches more of the barrel, he's a usable everyday outfielder on a contender; if it stays where it is, he's a two-win bench piece who plays above-average defense and not much else.

reports.published_report: The contact metrics are still elite — a 12.1% K%, a 20.0% chase rate, and a 12.5% whiff rate all hovering around the 93rd to 96th percentile range, but the power underneath them has quietly gone ordinary. His 38.2% hard-hit rate sits in the 37th percentile, and the .725 projected OPS reflects a hitter who wins with bat-to-ball now rather than the full offensive threat he was. At 33, this profile is a second-division regular leaning on discipline to stay relevant, valuable but no longer the engine of a lineup.

Seventy-five walks in 358 A+ plate appearances puts Luke Stevenson's BB% at 98th percentile among his peers, and the MLB-equivalent translates that to 14.0%, which is well above what most big-league hitters post. reports.name: Isaac Lyon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what makes this profile work, and what would unmake it. Across AA, A+, and A in 2026, Lyon is running a 2.8 BB/9 that translates to 3.2 at the MLB level, exactly matching the MLB average, which means the control edge he's leaning on right now is roughly a wash once the competition sharpens. The strikeout side is the honest problem: 8.4 K/9 in the minors becomes a 7.4 MLB-equivalent while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and without swing-and-miss to pair with the command, a 1.1 WHIP and 3.1 ERA across 84.3 innings looks more fragile than it reads. If the walk rate holds and the strikeouts nudge up as he faces better hitters, he's a back-end rotation piece; if the strikeouts stay where they are, what's left is a depth arm who has to be perfect to survive.

reports.name: Ryan Gallagher
reports.published_report: The walks are the whole argument. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Gallagher has issued 43 walks in 85.7 innings, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his BB/9 at 4.2 against a league context of 3.2 — stated differently, he's walking batters at a rate that would rank below the midpoint of any MLB rotation you'd want to write down. His 87 strikeouts are genuine production, but a K-BB% of 12% across the two levels translates to 10.7% at MLB equivalent, well short of the 13.5% MLB average, and the 5.8 ERA and 1.5 WHIP reflect what happens when the walks pile up behind hitters who can punish them. If the command tightens, you get a depth arm with enough strikeout volume to survive a rotation's back end; if it doesn't, the ceiling and the floor are the same thing.

reports.name: Jhonny Severino
reports.published_report: Twenty-seven home runs in 363 A+ plate appearances at age 21 is a number that demands attention, and the .301 ISO is deep into the 99th percentile of his pool. The translation, though, is where the profile gets complicated: that raw power likely translates to a .185 MLB-equivalent ISO, still above average, but his translated walk rate of 6.1% sits well short of the 8.5% MLB average and a 25.4% translated strikeout rate would play at the high end of acceptable. If the bat-to-ball shape doesn't sharpen as competition does, what's left is a right-handed corner bat whose power plays but whose hit tool leaves him exposed against advanced arms. Ceiling is a second-division regular if the power translates and the contact improves; floor is a bench piece whose strikeout and walk profile turns into a liability against anyone with a plan.

reports.name: Garret Forrester
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loud thing: 31 walks in 144 plate appearances across AAA & AA, which translates to a 13.0% BB% where the minor-league pool 99th-percentile mark tells you how far outside the norm that sits. That's a catcher with a genuine eye, and the .417 OBP and .500 SLG over that same stretch aren't decoration. The trouble is 144 PA is a thin foundation, the BABIP is only .252 so the contact isn't doing him favors, and the ceiling here is framed as organizational depth, not a regular. If the plate discipline holds and the ISO (.259 across AAA & AA, translating to .17 at the MLB level) survives the step up, he's a backup catcher who actually gets on base, which is more useful than the rank suggests — if it doesn't, the bat-to-ball (.241 average on a suppressed BABIP) doesn't carry him.

reports.name: Jared Serna
reports.published_report: The contact is the carrying tool. That's the one thing that plays at the next level without a question mark. reports.name: Kyle DeBarge
reports.published_report: The stolen bases are doing a lot of carrying here. Twenty-three swipes across 394 AA plate appearances keeps DeBarge relevant in the conversation, but a .207 average with a .261 BABIP isn't bad luck burying a real hitter — it's contact that doesn't find grass often enough and a 26% strikeout rate that translates to 27.3% against MLB arms, well above league average. The 45 walks are genuine, and the ISO translates to .130 at the equivalent MLB level, which is below-average pop for a second baseman you'd want in the lineup every day. If the speed remains elite and the contact improves just enough to stop the strikeouts from eating the lineup spot, he's a bench piece with real value on the bases; if it doesn't, he's organizational depth carrying a tool that only shows up when he actually gets on base.

reports.name: Eduardo Tait
reports.published_report: The ISO is the one thing propping this profile up, and it won't be enough. Tait is hitting .228 at A+ with 19 home runs in 410 plate appearances, which is a real number for a 19-year-old catcher, but the translation strips most of it away: the .214 raw ISO becomes .147 at the MLB level, right at league average, while a 24% strikeout rate at A+ becomes 27.5% against a MLB average of 22.0%, and his walk rate comes in below average too. The .253 BABIP tells you the contact isn't generating much even when it lands fair. If the power develops further as he grows into the position, there's a bench bat here; if the strikeout rate hardens and the ISO doesn't scale, he's organizational depth and not much more.

reports.name: Jose Escobar
reports.published_report: The .328/.400/.479 line across A+ & A is genuinely loud, but the translation mutes it fast. Escobar's contact rate is the real thing here, a 13% strikeout rate that translates to 18.8% in MLB context while most hitters sit at 22.0%, and his 37 walks show the plate discipline isn't just a BABIP story. The .369 BABIP is the number to watch; if that regresses hard, the ISO at .151 across A+ & A translates to just .117 at the MLB level, leaving a profile that's light on power and dependent on a hit-tool tested only at the lower minors. Either the contact and zone management carry him to a low-end regular, or the power ceiling keeps him a bench bat with a good average.

reports.name: Matt Ager
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working for him, and it isn't working hard enough to carry the rest. Across AA & A+, Ager has posted a 3.0 BB/9 that grades at the 85th percentile among his peers, but his 8.4 K/9 sits at just the 25th percentile, and the MLB translation makes the gap uglier: the strikeout rate moves to 7.4 while the walk rate essentially matches what MLB arms allow. A 14 K-BB% across 84 innings is functional, not a weapon. The profile hinges entirely on whether swing-and-miss materializes as he climbs, because if it doesn't, what's left is a strike-thrower without the stuff to make the strikes matter, which is a depth arm and nothing more.

reports.name: Dalton Pence
reports.published_report: The 2.9 ERA across AAA & AA & A+ is doing a lot of heavy lifting for a profile that doesn't translate cleanly to a rotation spot. Dalton Pence has logged 81.3 innings with a 1.2 WHIP and 92 strikeouts against 30 walks, and the control picture is genuinely better than the raw walk total suggests — his BB/9 sits in the 79th percentile of the pitcher pool, and a 19% K-BB% reflects real competitive balance. The MLB-equivalent translation puts him at roughly 8.3 K/9 and 3.5 BB/9, both essentially at league average, which means the ERA won't follow him north if the margins don't tighten. If the command holds and the strikeout rate finds another gear, there's a back-end starter or high-leverage arm in there; if it doesn't, what's left is a depth arm.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
